The early life stages of the littoral sea spider Pycnogonum litorale are characterized by exceptionally small body dimensions that match the species' cryptic existence among hydroid colonies. At hatching, the protonymphal stage emerges from the egg with a total length of only 0.015 cm [Lb = 0.015 cm], a scale that places the first free-swimming larva among the smallest of any pycnogonid. Subsequent development through a series of larval instars proceeds slowly, with each molt accompanied by incremental gains in body size. By the time the individual reaches the critical larval metamorphosis at the 5th larval instar, total length has increased to about 0.071 cm , marking the transition from the planktonic larval form to the benthic juvenile. Growth continues throughout the post-metamorphic juvenile phase, and maximum asymptotic size is attained only after many months. In adult females, the ultimate total length reaches approximately 1.01 cm [Li = approximately 1.01 cm], with field records indicating a range from 0.85 to 1.1 cm depending on local conditions and individual nutritional history.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the developmental timeline of P. litorale can be precisely delineated. Embryonic development from zygote formation to the emergence of the protonymphal larva requires approximately 32 days [ab = approximately 32 days], although incubation periods may vary between 32 and 81 days, with some records extending to a maximum of 111 days at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Following hatching, the planktonic larval phase persists until the completion of larval metamorphosis, which occurs at 83 days after birth , a duration that places the onset of the free-living benthic habit well within the first three months of life at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The transition to reproductive capability is considerably more protracted: sexual maturation, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and the attainment of puberty, is reached at 290 days after birth [tp = 290 days after birth] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This lengthy post-metamorphic juvenile period underscores the delayed reproductive strategy typical of this slow-growing invertebrate.

Reproductive output in P. litorale is striking given the animal's modest body size. At the same incubation temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], mature males gather fertilised ova into a compact brood mass carried on specialized ovigerous legs. Rough volumetric estimates, derived from photographic analyses suggesting the egg mass approximates the male's own body volume of about 0.05 cm³, indicate that each mass contains an extraordinary number of eggs. Given an individual egg diameter near the hatchling size, the total fecundity per reproductive event amounts to approximately 55,000 eggs per mass [N_R_i = approximately 55,000 eggs per mass]. This prodigious reproductive investment is deployed at a modest frequency; available observations suggest that males produce a single egg mass per year [F_R_i = single egg mass per year], a pattern consistent with the seasonally pulsed resources of the littoral habitat. The ultimate wet weight of an adult individual, estimated from a stylised body disc model as approximately 0.077 grams [Wwi = approximately 0.077 grams], further emphasizes the remarkable relative reproductive effort, with the egg load often exceeding the carrier's own mass.

The maximum recorded longevity for Pycnogonum litorale under constant thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] extends to roughly 9 years [am = roughly 9 years], a figure that places this species among the longer-lived pycnogonids studied to date. This extended lifespan, equivalent to over 3,285 days, allows for multiple annual reproductive opportunities over the course of a lifetime, though the slow juvenile development and late age at first reproduction suggest that individual lifetime reproductive success may be limited by environmental stochasticity. Senescence in sea spiders remains poorly documented, but the eventual physiological deterioration that culminates in organismal death in the ninth year likely reflects cumulative oxidative damage and the gradual exhaustion of somatic cell renewal capacity; the role of thermal stability in delaying this decline is an active area of investigation. By comparison, congeneric species in warmer waters exhibit shorter lifespans, supporting the view that temperature-driven metabolic rates are a primary determinant of longevity in this group.

Under the stable thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] that governs all developmental rates in this cold-water species, the transition to the pre-adult stage at the 8th juvenile instar occurs precisely when total length attains 0.82 cm [Lp = 0.82 cm]; this size is reached 290 days after birth [tp = 290 days after birth]. At this morphological threshold, the individual has completed the most dramatic phase of allometric shift, with the leg span expanding disproportionately relative to the trunk, a pattern that facilitates effective prey capture on colonial hydroids. This pre-adult size, although still well below the maximum adult dimensions, signals the onset of gametogenesis and the ability to engage in reproductive behaviour. Field surveys in North Atlantic littoral zones have documented that individuals attaining this size class also exhibit the secondary sexual characteristics necessary for mate recognition and ovigerous leg function. The time required to reach this size underscores the prolonged juvenile phase that characterizes the life history of this unassuming but biologically fascinating chelicerate.
